title: Laugh-induced seizure: a case report
case_prompt:
A 43-year-old obese Caucasian man with a history of insomnia, bipolar disorder, and chronic headache presented with multiple episodes of brief seizures, all induced by laughter when he watched comedy shows. He had experienced several mild episodes over the past month, each lasting approximately 5–10 seconds, characterized by the onset of laughter followed by arm shaking and a sensation that “his consciousness was being vacuumed away.” He denied tongue biting or incontinence. He averaged five episodes per day. There was no family history of seizure disorder.

On examination, he was alert and hemodynamically stable. Neurologic examination was normal. Serum electrolytes and glucose were within normal limits. A sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal. Brain MRI revealed an arachnoid cyst measuring 4.2 × 2.1 cm in the right anterior middle cranial fossa. He underwent two days of video EEG monitoring, which showed several bursts of generalized high-amplitude spike-and-wave activity with frontotemporal predominance, associated with staring, eye rolling, unresponsiveness, and tonic-clonic movements for 5–10 seconds, all provoked by deep, belly laughter; he reported complete lack of awareness during these episodes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bipolar disorder–related events — “All those manifestations were initially considered to be due to bipolar disorder and he had been maintained on valproic acid and topiramate for his chronic headaches, but this did not seem to be controlling his symptoms.”  
2. Drug-induced seizures (valproic acid) — “Other differentials included drug-induced seizures, mainly secondary to valproic acid, which was unlikely as the drug levels were normal. In addition, the patient continued to have seizure episodes even during the period of time he was off valproic acid.”  
3. Conversion disorder — “Conversion disorder was also considered but a two-day video EEG did reveal high-amplitude spikes.”  
4. Increased intracranial pressure from arachnoid cyst causing temporal lobe epilepsy — “Another diagnosis considered was increased intracranial pressure secondary to the arachnoid cyst, leading to compression of the right temporal lobe, triggering temporal lobe epilepsy. However, the video EEG did not display any discrete temporal lobe activities and his ventricles were normal sized on both computed tomography and MRI imaging of his brain.”  
5. Epileptic seizures provoked by laughter as a trigger — “He never had seizure activities without the context of laughter. Thus, it was felt much less likely that the patient displayed an epileptic seizure with laughter being one of the provoking factors.”  
6. Gelastic seizure — “Our case was distinct from gelastic seizure as laughter actually induced seizure activities that were recorded and confirmed by two-day video EEG.”
